expectedText:
FMLA LEAVE REQUEST & EMPLOYER NOTICE
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

WHO IS ELIGIBLE
Jordan Lee is eligible for FMLA leave only if Jordan Lee has worked for Acme, Inc. for at least 12 months, has worked at least 1,250 hours for Acme, Inc. in the preceding 12-month period, and works at a location where Acme, Inc. employs at least 50 employees within 75 miles.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-30]
  "The term “eligible employee” means an employee who has been employed— (i) for at least 12 months by the employer with respect to whom leave is requested under section 2612 of this title; and (ii) for at least 1,250 hours of service with such employer during the previous 12-month period."
  — 29 U.S.C. § 2611(2)(A) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Family and Medical Leave Act, eligible-employee definition (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/29/2611)
  "any employee of an employer who is employed at a worksite at which such employer employs less than 50 employees if the total number of employees employed by that employer within 75 miles of that worksite is less than 50."
  — 29 U.S.C. § 2611(2)(B)(ii) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Family and Medical Leave Act, worksite-size exclusion (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/29/2611)
  Known gap: These three conditions are cumulative — missing any one of them means the employee isn't eligible under this federal law, regardless of how long they've worked there or how compelling the reason for leave is. This document doesn't determine eligibility for a specific case; it states the test.

LEAVE ENTITLEMENT
An eligible employee is entitled to 12 workweeks of leave during any 12-month period for the birth of a child and to care for the newborn; the placement of a child for adoption or foster care; to care for a spouse, child, or parent with a serious health condition; or because of the employee's own serious health condition that makes the employee unable to perform the job.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "an eligible employee shall be entitled to a total of 12 workweeks of leave during any 12-month period for one or more of the following: (A) Because of the birth of a son or daughter of the employee and in order to care for such son or daughter. (B) Because of the placement of a son or daughter with the employee for adoption or foster care. (C) In order to care for the spouse, or a son, daughter, or parent, of the employee, if such spouse, son, daughter, or parent has a serious health condition. (D) Because of a serious health condition that makes the employee unable to perform the functions of the position of such employee."
  — 29 U.S.C. § 2612(a)(1)(A)-(D) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Family and Medical Leave Act, leave entitlement (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/29/2612)
  "Except in the case of leave to care for a covered servicemember with a serious injury or illness, an eligible employee's FMLA leave entitlement is limited to a total of 12 workweeks of leave during any 12-month period for any one, or more, of the following reasons: (1) The birth of the employee's son or daughter, and to care for the newborn child; (2) The placement with the employee of a son or daughter for adoption or foster care, and to care for the newly placed child; (3) To care for the employee's spouse, son, daughter, or parent with a serious health condition; (4) Because of a serious health condition that makes the employee unable to perform one or more of the essential functions"
  — 29 C.F.R. § 825.200(a) (Cornell LII text), Electronic Code of Federal Regulations, DOL's own restatement of the 12-workweek entitlement (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/29/825.200)
  Known gap: This describes the four most commonly used qualifying reasons under this provision. Two more categories exist under this same law that this document doesn't cover: leave for a qualifying exigency arising from a family member's covered active military duty, and up to 26 workweeks — not 12 — in a single 12-month period to care for a covered servicemember family member.

MILITARY FAMILY LEAVE
Two additional, separate categories of leave exist under the same law for military families. First, an eligible employee can take leave — still within the general 12-workweek entitlement — for a qualifying exigency arising from a spouse's, child's, or parent's covered active duty (or call to active duty) in the Armed Forces; the specific qualifying exigencies are defined by regulation, not this statute directly. Second, an eligible employee who is the spouse, child, parent, or next of kin of a covered servicemember can take up to 26 workweeks — more than double the general entitlement — in a single 12-month period to care for that servicemember, though this longer leave is available only once, not in every 12-month period.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-31]
  "Because of any qualifying exigency (as the Secretary shall, by regulation, determine) arising out of the fact that the spouse, or a son, daughter, or parent of the employee is on covered active duty (or has been notified of an impending call or order to covered active duty) in the Armed Forces."
  — 29 U.S.C. § 2612(a)(1)(E) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Family and Medical Leave Act, qualifying exigency leave (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/29/2612)
  "an eligible employee who is the spouse, son, daughter, parent, or next of kin of a covered servicemember shall be entitled to a total of 26 workweeks of leave during a 12-month period to care for the servicemember. The leave described in this paragraph shall only be available during a single 12-month period."
  — 29 U.S.C. § 2612(a)(3) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Family and Medical Leave Act, servicemember family leave (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/29/2612)
  Known gap: This is a real, quotable federal entitlement, not a summary — verified against the current U.S. Code text. If an employee takes both the general 12-workweek leave and the 26-week servicemember caregiver leave in the same single 12-month period, the combined total is still capped at 26 workweeks, not 38. This document doesn't state the regulatory definition of a qualifying exigency, which is set by the Department of Labor, not the statute itself.

LEAVE REQUEST
Jordan Lee requests FMLA leave as described below.

Reason for leave: _______________________________________________
Requested start date: _______________
Expected return date: _______________
Intermittent or reduced schedule (if applicable): _______________________________________________

RETURNING FROM LEAVE
When Jordan Lee returns from FMLA leave taken for its intended purpose, Acme, Inc. must restore Jordan Lee to the same position held before the leave, or to an equivalent position with equivalent pay, benefits, and other terms and conditions of employment. Taking FMLA leave doesn't cause Jordan Lee to lose any employment benefit that had already accrued before the leave began.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-30]
  "any eligible employee who takes leave under section 2612 of this title for the intended purpose of the leave shall be entitled, on return from such leave— (A) to be restored by the employer to the position of employment held by the employee when the leave commenced; or (B) to be restored to an equivalent position with equivalent employment benefits, pay, and other terms and conditions of employment. ... The taking of leave under section 2612 of this title shall not result in the loss of any employment benefit accrued prior to the date on which the leave commenced."
  — 29 U.S.C. § 2614(a)(1)-(2) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Family and Medical Leave Act, restoration to position (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/29/2614)
  "Nothing in this section shall be construed to entitle any restored employee to— (A) the accrual of any seniority or employment benefits during any period of leave; or (B) any right, benefit, or position of employment other than any right, benefit, or position to which the employee would have been entitled had the employee not taken the leave."
  — 29 U.S.C. § 2614(a)(3) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Family and Medical Leave Act, limitations on restoration (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/29/2614)
  "An employer may deny restoration under subsection (a) to any eligible employee described in paragraph (2) if— (A) such denial is necessary to prevent substantial and grievous economic injury to the operations of the employer; (B) the employer notifies the employee of the intent of the employer to deny restoration on such basis at the time the employer determines that such injury would occur; and (C) in any case in which the leave has commenced, the employee elects not to return to employment after receiving such notice. ... An eligible employee described in paragraph (1) is a salaried eligible employee who is among the highest paid 10 percent of the employees employed by the employer within 75 miles of the facility at which the employee is employed."
  — 29 U.S.C. § 2614(b) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Family and Medical Leave Act, highly compensated employee exemption (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/29/2614)
  Known gap: This restoration right has two real limits. First, it doesn't entitle a returning employee to accrue seniority or benefits during the leave itself, or to any right, benefit, or position better than what the employee would have had without taking leave — restoration is a floor, not an upgrade. Second, federal law lets an employer deny restoration to certain highly compensated employees — those among the highest-paid 10% within 75 miles of the facility — if restoring them would cause substantial and grievous economic injury to the business, the employer notifies the employee of that intent when it determines the injury would occur, and, if leave has already started, the employee still chooses not to return after receiving that notice.

NO INTERFERENCE OR RETALIATION
Acme, Inc. will not interfere with, restrain, or deny Jordan Lee's exercise of rights under this law, and will not discharge or discriminate against Jordan Lee for opposing a practice this law makes unlawful.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-30]
  "It shall be unlawful for any employer to interfere with, restrain, or deny the exercise of or the attempt to exercise, any right provided under this subchapter. ... It shall be unlawful for any employer to discharge or in any other manner discriminate against any individual for opposing any practice made unlawful by this subchapter."
  — 29 U.S.C. § 2615(a) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Family and Medical Leave Act, interference with rights (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/29/2615)
  "It shall be unlawful for any person to discharge or in any other manner discriminate against any individual because such individual— (1) has filed any charge, or has instituted or caused to be instituted any proceeding, under or related to this subchapter; (2) has given, or is about to give, any information in connection with any inquiry or proceeding relating to any right provided under this subchapter; or (3) has testified, or is about to testify, in any inquiry or proceeding relating to any right provided under this subchapter."
  — 29 U.S.C. § 2615(b) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Family and Medical Leave Act, interference with proceedings or inquiries (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/29/2615)
  Known gap: This protection extends beyond someone who actually takes leave — it also covers interference with the attempt to exercise a right under this law, and separately protects anyone who has filed a charge, given information, or testified in a proceeding related to it, not just the person who requested leave.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
Please sign below to acknowledge this leave request and the terms above.

Employee: Jordan Lee
Date: _______________
